text: Taped to the back of the Minox, in Madame Novak's handwriting: "In trouble in Istanbul, darling? Rıza, carpets, the Grand Bazaar. Show him this camera. Z."
She thinks of everything. She probably knew I'd end up in Istanbul before I did.
Nightglass Seven, ticking as it cools. Five hours in its equipment bay with a goose. I will never fly again. I may never eat again.
The tea boy, fast asleep on his stool. In Istanbul, tea boys are everywhere, carry tea to everyone, and see everything. This one is seeing the inside of his eyelids.
Çay... çay... two sugars... zzz...
A brass tray with six glasses of tea, still hot. Nobody in Istanbul ever questions a man carrying tea.
I'll bring it back. Probably.
A kettle on a kettle, the Turkish way. Somewhere there is always tea brewing, even in a secret hangar at six in the morning.
GİRİLMEZ: no entry. PRIVATE HANGAR. I'm not so much entering as leaving.
Vasko threw the catalogue on the floor. He's read it. He's in it. It's excellent.
LOT ONE: NIGHTGLASS. Tonight at nine, at Bay Selim's yalı. Three buyers and a telephone. One of them is a Monsieur Dupont of Marseille, "who is never seen".
A buyer nobody has ever seen. Now there's a man I could be.
An airfield guard with a moustache like a yard brush and the expression of a man who has been awake since four.
Go, go! And tell the kitchen: more sugar next time.
Dur! Stop! Papers! This is a private airfield. Nobody leaves without a pass. Nobody arrives without a pass. Nobody even has a pass.
He's been standing there since four in the morning. And there's a tea boy asleep right behind me.
Dur! Where are you going, baker? Papers!
Colonel Vasko! Welcome to Istanbul. Your aircraft arrived without a sound. Only a strange honking.
The engines. They will be adjusted. Bay Selim, the buyers?
Three, Colonel. A banker from Zürich, an oil man from Houston, and Monsieur Dupont of Marseille, whom nobody has ever seen. And the telephone line to London, as you asked.
Excellent. Tonight at nine, at your yalı. Captain Kolar will stand at the door.
The catalogue, Colonel.
I have read it. I am in it. It is excellent.
Five hours in the equipment bay of a supersonic aircraft, with a goose. Istanbul. I think. Everything is still spinning.
Colonel, if you are ever sick on me again, it's the oven.
Çay, abi. Tea, sir. With the compliments of the kitchen.
Tea! At last! Four hours I stand here, and nobody brings tea!
Ahh. Two sugars. Perfect. Go, go, tea boy. Tell the kitchen I love them.
A man carrying tea can walk through any door in Istanbul. I must write that down for Technical Section.
The Grand Bazaar. Four thousand shops, sixty-one streets, and every one of them has a man who wants to sell me a carpet.
Kilims from Konya, silk from Hereke. Every carpet here has a story, and Rıza will tell it to you for three hours.
A whole wall of glass lanterns, glowing like boiled sweets. Somewhere, a man is trying to sell one to a German tourist for a thousand marks. He will succeed.
Saffron, sumac, pul biber and something labelled "Sultan's Aphrodisiac". I'll pass.
Lokum: rose, lemon, pistachio. Soft as a pillow and sweet enough to stop your heart.
The man behind the counter is watching me with the eyes of a hawk. A hawk who has had things stolen before.
A carpet dealer in a waistcoat, glasses on the end of his nose, and the patient smile of a man who has never once sold a carpet for the first price he said.
Selim's catalogue. Beautiful paper. Terrible business.
I do not read the catalogues of strangers, effendi.
I don't even know where I'm going yet. Rıza is the man to ask.
The Beyazıt Gate, back out into the city. Not yet.
The hammam is down the lane, past the goldsmiths. Give Mustafa the lokum, and go with God, effendi. And with the goose.
Hoş geldiniz! Welcome! You need a carpet. Everybody needs a carpet. You, effendi, need two carpets and a very long bath.
I'm looking for Rıza.
Many men are looking for Rıza. Most of them want money back. What does a baker's boy with a goose want?
Madame Novak must have known him. Maybe there's something about him on her camera.
"Show him this camera," she wrote.
Still here, baker? Buy a carpet or show me something interesting.
A friend lent me this camera. She said you'd know it.
Zdenka's Minox! Allah allah. She photographed my wedding. And then my divorce. Same photographer, much better pictures.
Any friend of Zdenka is a friend of Rıza. What do you need, effendi?
I need to get into Bay Selim's yalı tonight. There's an auction.
Selim's auctions! Only buyers with invitations. And the buyers spend the afternoon at the Çemberlitaş hammam, because a man in a towel cannot hide a microphone.
One of the buyers is a Monsieur Dupont, of Marseille. Whom nobody has ever seen.
Dupont! Every sale, three hours on the marble, face down, with a cloth over his head. Mustafa the masseur says his back is magnificent. Nobody knows his face.
Mustafa is my cousin. He will do anything for rose lokum. Take this box.
And Zdenka left this for you, in case you came. A tulip, with a very small ear in it. Put it by their telephone, and she can trace who is on the other end.
Rıza, how can I ever repay you?
Buy a carpet. Not today. One day. A big one.
Bay Selim wants six carpets for the auction room, and they must be red, and...
YOU! The baker's boy! From the mountain! HARROW!
Rıza! Which way to the hammam?
Left, right, left, past the goldsmiths! Run, effendi!
Star-shaped holes in the dome, letting in columns of light through the steam. Four hundred years old. Better ventilation than MI6.
Marble basins, brass taps, and little brass bowls for pouring hot water over your head. And then cold water. And then screaming.
Locker seven, empty now, and locker twelve, with a baker's smock in it that I hope never to see again.
Numbered lockers. Twelve is mine, with a floury smock in it. Seven belongs to Monsieur Dupont.
Nuri, keeper of the lockers. He has worked here for sixty years and remembers every towel.
Monsieur Dupont, pummelled into a coma of relaxation, snoring into the marble.
A man lying face down on the hot marble, a red towel round his middle and a cloth over his head. Monsieur Dupont of Marseille, whom nobody has ever seen. Including me, so far.
Zzz... oui... encore... zzz...
Monsieur Dupont?
Non. Go away. I am relaxing. Nobody has seen my face since 1971, and I am not starting again for a baker in a towel.
Dupont's locker token, dangling off the marble on its rubber band.
Number seven. Pardon, monsieur. I'll bring it back when I've finished being you.
Mustafa the masseur: seven feet of muscle and moustache. He is kneading Dupont like a man making bread for a hundred people.
The Sultan's Special. Very strong. He will wake up tomorrow, very happy, very flat.
Massage? Later, friend. First Monsieur Dupont. He pays by the hour, and he has booked three.
What would it take to finish him off early?
The Sultan's Special. Very strong. Very good. Very painful. But I only do it for a very good reason. Rose lokum is a very good reason.
Not like this. I need an invitation, and a better outfit than a towel.
I think I lost him at the goldsmiths. Or he lost me. Either way, I'm in a bathhouse.
Welcome, welcome! But not like that. Nobody goes into the hot room dressed like a bakery. Clothes off, towel on.
And the goose?
She's with me.
Geese bathe for free on Tuesdays. Today is Tuesday. She is lucky.
A red checked towel and nothing else. If Control could see me now, I'd be demoted to Accounts.
Goodbye, Monsieur Dupont. You look taller than you did this morning.
You want your locker, twelve? The smock is quite safe. I have folded it. It was not easy.
What about locker seven?
Seven is Monsieur Dupont's. Only the man with the token opens seven. Sixty years, nobody opens a locker without a token. Not even me. Especially not me.
Rose lokum, from your cousin Rıza. And a very good reason.
Rıza's lokum! The best in Istanbul! For this, Monsieur Dupont gets the Sultan's Special. On the house.
Oh là là! Oh là là là là!
Oh... that is... magnifique... zzz.
Finished. He will wake tomorrow. Very happy. Very flat.
And his locker token is dangling off the edge of the marble.
Seven. Monsieur Dupont. Hm. You look taller when you are standing up.
It's the steam.
A dinner jacket, an invitation to the Yalı Selim, and, in a little velvet box, a false moustache. For when he has to meet people.
Bonsoir. I am Monsieur Dupont of Marseille. Nobody has ever seen me, and tonight nobody will see me again.
Very handsome. The moustache is a little crooked.
The Bosphorus at night: the bridge lit up like a necklace, Europe on one side and Asia on the other. And me in the middle, in somebody else's moustache.
A photograph of Nightglass on an easel, lit like a film star. LOT ONE. No reserve.
Leyla, standing on a chair, screaming at a goose.
Leyla, Bay Selim's secretary, sitting by the telephone like a hen on an egg. The line to London is open.
Get it away! Get it away from me!
Good evening, Monsieur Dupont. The line to London is for the telephone bidder only. Nobody may touch the telephone. Nobody may even look at it.
Who is the telephone bidder?
I only know his voice, monsieur. Very English. He stirs his tea very loudly.
An ivory telephone with a gold dial and a line straight to London. Leyla hasn't taken her eyes off it all evening.
The tulip is in place. Madame Novak is listening.
Monsieur! Please! Do not touch the telephone!
Monsieur! A flower? For me? How kind. But please, not near the telephone.
Vasko, in full dress uniform with every medal he owns. Tonight he becomes a very rich man. He is practising looking modest in the window. It isn't working.
Monsieur Dupont. At last. Tonight you will see the finest aircraft ever built, and the finest man ever to build it.
Mm. And which one is for sale?
...Only the aircraft.
Herr Brunner of Zürich, a banker with a face like a closed safe.
Good evening. I do not discuss money before an auction. After an auction, I do not discuss anything.
Mr Hollis of Houston: a white hat, a red face, and a wallet you could land a plane on.
Howdy, Frenchy! I aim to buy me an invisible airplane. Trouble is, I can't find the dang thing.
Bay Selim, host and auctioneer. A white dinner jacket and the smile of a man who takes ten per cent of everything.
Monsieur Dupont! Please, take your seat. We begin when all our guests are seated.
Not before I've put Madame Novak's tulip by that telephone.
Kolar at the door. He keeps looking at me as if he's trying to remember where he left his keys.
Monsieur Dupont. Have we... no. No. Enjoy the auction, monsieur.
A gilt chair with a card: M. DUPONT. And a numbered paddle, thirteen. Lucky for somebody.
Not yet. The tulip goes by the telephone first, or this whole evening is for nothing.
Invitation.
Dupont. Of Marseille.
Monsieur Dupont... have we met?
Non. Nobody has met me. It is my whole personality.
...Welcome, monsieur.
Monsieur Dupont! At last, a face to the name. And such a moustache!
The telephone is on the left, with a secretary guarding it. And the goose is out on the terrace, sulking.
A GOOSE! There is a goose in the salon! Get it away from me!
Yee-haw! Now that's what I call a floor show!
Captain! Remove that bird!
I know that goose...
Leyla's on a chair across the room. The telephone is all mine.
One enamel tulip, tucked behind the telephone. Madame Novak, you have a line to London.
Got you! Out you go, bird. Back on the terrace.
Thank you, Captain. I am quite all right. I am... quite all right.
Ladies and gentlemen. Lot One: Nightglass. Invisible to radar, and very nearly to the naked eye. The Colonel will say a few words.
It is magnificent. So am I. We begin at ten million dollars.
Eleven!
Twelve.
Monsieur Dupont?
Fifteen million.
Fifteen million, from Monsieur Dupont!
Is that in dollars, or in lira?
Dollars, monsieur. In lira we would be here until Thursday.
Then, fifteen million.
Nobody bids by scratching their nose. That only happens in films.
Twenty million! From Monsieur Dupont!
Apparently it also happens in Istanbul.
Twenty-five! Dang it, twenty-five!
Thirty.
Thirty million, from Herr Brunner. Monsieur Dupont?
Forty million!
Dupont's deposit is twenty million francs and a spare moustache. I hope nobody checks.
Thirty-five million, and a box of Turkish delight.
The Turkish delight is noted. Thirty-five million!
Don't move. Don't sneeze. Don't touch the moustache.
I see Monsieur Dupont's moustache has twitched. Forty million!
The telephone bids... fifty million dollars.
Fifty? Well, shoot. I'm out. I'll buy Texas instead.
I do not bid against telephones. Telephones do not pay their bills.
Fifty million on the telephone. Monsieur Dupont?
If I say fifty-one, somebody asks for the money. And all I have is a Minox, a moustache and a goose.
Monsieur Dupont... declines.
Going... going... gone! Sold, to the gentleman on the telephone, for fifty million dollars!
Magnificent. As predicted. By me.
One moment. The gentleman on the telephone has one more request.
He says he will take the goose as well. The one called Colonel.
Nobody in this room knows that goose's name. Only Ilse, Anička, Madame Novak...
...and whoever Madame Novak tells her secrets to, on the telephone, every Sunday. In London. Stirring his tea very loudly.
The terrace, the Bosphorus, and the Colonel, banished, glaring at the seagulls.
Ships going north to the Black Sea and south to the Mediterranean, and the bridge between two continents. Istanbul does everything twice.
A fast little motor boat, keys in the ignition. Somebody here is expecting to leave in a hurry. It might be me.
The Colonel, thrown out for the second time tonight. She looks very pleased with herself.
The Colonel, banished to the terrace by the footman. She is sulking magnificently.
You've done enough, Colonel. Stay here and guard the boat.
Colonel. There's a secretary inside who is terrified of birds, and a telephone I need to get near. Are you in?
I'll take that as a yes.
Madame Novak's Minox has something taped to the back. I should look at it properly.
Vasko threw the auction catalogue on the floor by the jet.
That guard has been standing there since four. He looks like a man who needs tea.
The tea boy is asleep, and his tray of tea is sitting right beside him.
The gate is open to a tea boy. Off to the Grand Bazaar.
"Show him this camera," Madame Novak wrote. Rıza, the carpet dealer.
The carpet dealer might be the man I need. Madame Novak's Minox has a note on it.
The hammam is down the lane on the right.
Mustafa would do anything for rose lokum, Rıza said. Including finishing Dupont off early.
Dupont's locker token is dangling off the marble.
Nuri opens a locker for anyone with the right token.
Monsieur Dupont has an auction to go to. The door is on the right.
Leyla won't leave that telephone. She needs something to be more frightened of than Bay Selim. Something with feathers, out on the terrace.
Leyla's on a chair. The tulip, by the telephone, now.
My seat is waiting. Paddle thirteen.
The Colonel is sulking by the balustrade. Time she earned her keep.
Into the salon with the Colonel.
Nothing special.
That won't work.
I don't think so.
Not a chance.
That doesn't help here.
Those two don't go together.
Stop that baker!
Excuse me! Sorry! Mind the carpets!
Disguised as the village baker's boy, Jack photographed Nightglass inside the mountain, found Vasko's flight plan, and hid in the aircraft's equipment bay a moment before it took off for Istanbul.
Five hours in a freezing, roaring, pitch-black box, with a goose. Neither of them enjoyed it.
Dawn on the Asian shore. Tonight Colonel Vasko sells Nightglass to the highest bidder.
In a flat above the Graben, Madame Novak takes off her headphones, very slowly, and puts down her cup of tea.
Going, going, gone.
Chapter Six: Masquerade.
Madame Novak's Minox, with thirty-six photographs of Nightglass inside. And a slip of paper taped to the back.

LOT ONE: NIGHTGLASS. Buyers: Herr Brunner of Zürich. Mr Hollis of Houston. Monsieur Dupont of Marseille, "who is never seen". And a telephone line to London. Buyers are the guests of the Çemberlitaş hammam before the sale.
A brass tray with six tulip glasses of tea. In Istanbul, a man carrying tea can walk through any door in the city.
A box of rose-flavoured Turkish delight, dusted with sugar. Mustafa the masseur would do anything for it, says Rıza.
An enamel tulip with a very small microphone in it. Madame Novak's. Put it near their telephone, and she can trace the call.
A brass token on a rubber band. Number seven: Monsieur Dupont's locker.
Bay Selim requests the pleasure of Monsieur J. Dupont at the Yalı Selim, Kandilli, at nine o'clock. Black tie. No cameras. No geese.
The evening ferry to Kandilli. A man in a dinner jacket and a false moustache stands at the rail, sharing a sesame simit with a goose, and fighting off the seagulls.
A wooden palace on the water, every window lit. Captain Kolar at the door, checking invitations. And a footman, who takes one look at the goose and points at the terrace.
